column4: The parallel («blue») dollar trades far above the official rate. Exporters hold back their harvest, importers rush their purchases and prices adjust to the dearer dollar.
The central bank has almost no dollars of its own. It cannot defend the peso, cannot pay for energy and parts imports, and every debt payment becomes a crisis.
Argentine bonds yield thousands of basis points above US Treasuries. Nobody lends, companies cannot get credit and the debt becomes unpayable.
Everyone wants dollars at once. The price jumps day after day, shops mark up prices and the central bank burns reserves to stop the stampede.
Banks cap withdrawals of deposits. Savers bang pots on bank shutters and the economy grinds to a halt.
The country stops paying its foreign debt. International credit is cut off for years and a long renegotiation with bondholders and holdout funds begins.
Grassroots groups and the unemployed block roads, bridges and avenues every day to demand jobs, food and welfare.
The labour federation calls general strikes and mass marches. Transport stops, factories close and the government gets a clear message.
Gas runs short in winter and power in summer. The country imports LNG cargoes at a fortune and industry faces scheduled cuts.
The country is split into two halves that do not listen to each other. Every measure is a battle and half the electorate will never vote for you.
Good weather and good prices: soybeans, corn and wheat yield like never before and dollars pour in through the port of Rosario.
Vaca Muerta is producing at full tilt. Argentina goes from importing gas to exporting energy, and the energy balance brings in dollars for the first time in years.
Low inflation, a steady dollar and rising reserves. For the first time in a long while, Argentines can plan more than a month ahead.
The official dollar jumps overnight. Shelf prices are marked up within days: food, medicine and rents adjust to the new exchange rate.
Wages and pensions trail prices. Families cut back on meat, outings and medicine, and run up credit card debt to reach the end of the month.
Shops sell less, factories run at half capacity and construction has stalled. The economy slides into recession.
With a strong peso, the country becomes pricey in dollar terms: holidays in Brazil and shopping in Chile are cheaper, cheap imports pour in and local industry loses competitiveness.

column4: Workshops, textile mills and shops close their doors. They cannot compete with imports or pay utility bills, interest and rent while sales fall.
Formal jobs are lost every month. Odd jobs, delivery apps and despair in poor neighbourhoods grow.
Monthly inflation falls month after month. Instalment credit, mortgages and the ability to compare prices come back.
For the first time in years, the state spends less than it collects. There is no longer a need to print money to pay salaries.
Big projects arrive: pipelines, copper and lithium mines, data centres and ports. The provinces compete to attract them.
Residents and specialists at national hospitals strike over pay. Surgeries are rescheduled and patients' families march alongside the doctors.
Providers paid months late, pensions cancelled and centres closing. Families rally outside Congress.
Lecturers on rock-bottom pay, open-air classes in squares and faculty occupations. The university community becomes the main hub of opposition.
Every Wednesday, pensioners march to Congress over pensions that do not stretch. Images of police crackdowns travel around the world.
The opposition and the governors join forces: they override vetoes, reject decrees and block the budget.
Leaked audio, court cases and raids every week. Each new revelation erodes support even among the government's own voters.
A high-intensity war in Eastern Europe sends oil, gas and grain prices soaring. Argentine farmers sell at higher prices; imported inflation hits household budgets.
War in the Persian Gulf partly closes the Strait of Hormuz. Oil soars: Asia scrambles for suppliers and Vaca Muerta finds buyers.
The US and China trade tariffs. Argentine steel and aluminium face surcharges, but China buys more South American soybeans to avoid depending on the US.
The Federal Reserve raises rates. Capital flows back to Wall Street, emerging markets pay more to borrow and Argentine country risk rebounds.
Brazil, the main buyer of Argentine cars and manufactures, devalues the real and slides into recession. Car plants suspend shifts.
Soybeans, corn, lithium and copper trade at highs. Dollars pour in as in 2008.
A new virus spreads around the world. Closed borders, overwhelmed hospitals and an economy on hold.
A Wall Street crash freezes world credit. Investors flee anything that looks risky, starting with Argentina.
The crisis in Venezuela and violence elsewhere push hundreds of thousands of people towards Argentina.
After 25 years of talks, the Mercosur-EU agreement takes effect: beef, wine and lemons enter Europe tariff-free.
